text: A decision tree predicts the way a checklist does. Ask a yes-or-no question about one feature, follow the branch, ask another, and repeat until you reach an answer. Trees are easy to read, need little preparation, and are the building block of the most powerful tabular models.

Training is greedy and recursive. Try every feature and every split point. Pick the split that makes the two groups purest, measured by Gini impurity, which is zero for a perfectly pure group. Repeat inside each group. Each final group, called a leaf, predicts its most common class.

Here's a tree on eight hundred illustrative customers. New customers, heavy support users, and high bills churn more. Fitting with max depth three gives point seven eight eight on training data and point seven eight three on test. Always predicting stay would score point six two nine, so the tree adds real signal.

This is the output of the code above. The root asks whether tenure is at most eleven and a half. Each box shows its Gini score, its row counts, and its majority class. Follow any customer down and you have an explanation in plain questions. That's the tree's biggest strength.

Now remove the depth limit. The tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure. Training accuracy is a perfect one point oh, with eighteen levels and a hundred fifty-six leaves. But test accuracy drops to point seven one two, worse than the small tree. That's memorization.

The trade-offs. Trees are interpretable, need no scaling, and capture non-linear effects and interactions automatically. But they overfit unless constrained, they're unstable, since small data changes can produce a very different tree, and their predictions are step-like rather than smooth.
That instability is exactly what the next lesson fixes, by combining many trees. Next up: random forests.
